lesson.title: ARP: Finding a MAC Address for an IP Address
lesson.summary: ARP is the protocol IPv4 hosts on the same local network use to discover the MAC address behind a known IP address, which is the missing piece needed to actually deliver a frame on the wire.
lesson.body:
Sending data to a device on your own local network requires two different addresses working together, and they operate at different layers for different reasons. The IP address identifies a device logically and is what routing decisions are based on. The MAC address identifies a device's network interface physically and is what an Ethernet or Wi-Fi frame actually needs in its header to be delivered to the right hardware on a shared local network. A host can easily know the IP address of another device on its network, perhaps its default gateway, without having any idea what MAC address belongs to that IP. ARP, the Address Resolution Protocol, exists to close that gap.

ARP works through a simple request and reply exchange. A host that needs a MAC address for a known IP address sends an ARP request, and it sends this request as an Ethernet broadcast, addressed to every device on the local network at once, essentially asking who has this IP address and asking them to say so. Every device on the network receives the broadcast, but only the one that actually holds that IP address is supposed to answer. That device replies directly to the requester, not as a broadcast this time but as a normal, one to one unicast frame, with an ARP reply that states its own MAC address. The requester then stores this IP to MAC mapping in a local ARP cache for a period of time, so it does not have to repeat the broadcast for every packet it sends to that same neighbor.

Picture a laptop at 192.168.1.10 that wants to send traffic out to the internet through its gateway at 192.168.1.1. The laptop knows the gateway's IP address, because that was handed to it by DHCP, but it has no idea what MAC address sits behind that IP, and it cannot build an Ethernet frame without one. It broadcasts an ARP request asking who has 192.168.1.1. The router recognizes its own address, and replies directly to the laptop with an ARP reply carrying its MAC address, something like 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e. The laptop caches that mapping, builds an Ethernet frame addressed to that MAC, and every packet it sends toward the internet for the next several minutes can skip the broadcast step entirely and go straight to that cached MAC address.

ARP only exists for IPv4, and it sits in an unusual spot in the layering model, since it resolves a network layer address into a link layer address and its request and reply frames travel directly over Ethernet rather than being carried inside an IP packet, which is why it is sometimes described as operating at layer two and a half. It also only ever works within a single local network, since broadcasts do not cross routers, which is exactly why a host needs to resolve its gateway's MAC address rather than the MAC address of some distant server on the other side of the internet. IPv6 abandons ARP entirely in favor of a different mechanism built on ICMPv6, which the next chapter covers.
